headline: Holgate's New Cut Found the Bluefish First — Fluke Sliding Into the Inlet Rips
subhead: A storm-carved slough at Holgate turned into a bait trap this week, and the bunker blitz we flagged last week showed up right on schedule.
body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate stretch Tuesday morning at first light and the beach looked different than it did two weeks ago — that happens fast down there. A modest south swell over the weekend cut a new slough about 200 yards north of the refuge fence, carved a trough maybe four feet deep at low tide with a sandbar humped up on the seaward side. That kind of structure doesn't sit empty for long on LBI in late July. By Wednesday there was bunker stacked in that trough thick enough to color the water bronze, and the bluefish found it before I did — I heard the pop of a blitz from the parking lot before I even had my waders on.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the bunker-driven blitz working up from South Jersey would find LBI and intensify inside 48 to 72 hours, and that's exactly what's happened. The bait pods are riding the warm surface layer right along the beachfront from Holgate up through Beach Haven and into Ship Bottom, and the bluefish are pinning them against the new cuts and bars on the moving tide. Best windows have been the first hour of light and the last hour before dark, which lines up with when the light drops enough that the blues stop spooking off the pods and start slashing through them. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Hopkins, anything in the 1.5 to 2 ounce range that you can bomb into the melee — have been the move. If you can match the bunker size with a bigger paddletail swimbait, even better; the blues aren't picky when the bait's balled up that tight.

Fluke have gone the other direction, and it's a pattern I see every summer once the flats hit the mid-70s. The open bay drifts inside Manahawkin and Little Egg Harbor have gone quiet — too warm, too slow-moving — and the fish have slid into the current seams where the water actually moves and stays a few degrees cooler. Barnegat Inlet and Beach Haven Inlet are carrying the load right now. I've had my best luck working the deeper bends on the channel side of Beach Haven Inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing, dragging 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet right along the bottom where the current stacks bait against the drop-off. Nothing huge — most fish are running 17 to 20 inches — but there's enough of them stacked in that seam to make a short drift worth repeating six or eight times in a tide. Little Egg Inlet is fishing similarly on the ebb, especially the deeper hole just inside the rock jetty, though you're fighting boat traffic there on weekends.

Striped bass are basically nocturnal at this point, and that's not going to change until the water cools off in September. Surface temps along the beachfront and in the back bays are sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, which pushes bass deep and shuts down any real daytime activity except on the edges of structure where there's a thermocline to hide in. The play after dark has been bridge structure — the Route 72 causeway pilings and the Manahawkin Bay Bridge abutments — working bucktail eels and fresh bunker chunks tight to the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing. A few guys working the Barnegat Light rocks after midnight with darter-style plugs have connected on schoolie-to-mid-20s fish working the current seam off the jetty tip, but you need to be out there at 11 p.m. or later, and even then it's a few fish a trip, not a blitz. That's the honest state of it right now — the bass are there, they're just not stupid in this heat.

Black drum season wrapped up back in June — that Mullica and Graveling Point bite on the incoming tide is done for the year, don't waste a trip on it. What's interesting is the weakfish. I've had a couple reports of weakfish showing after dark in the deeper holes off Graveling Point and up into the Mullica proper, fish in the 16 to 19 inch range hitting bucktails tipped with squid strips on the bottom of the outgoing. It's not a fishery yet, more a handful of fish here and there, but it's worth a look if you're already out there chasing bass at night — bring an extra rod rigged light.

Kingfish are the one bright spot for the sand-spike crowd. Bloodworms and Fishbites on high-low rigs have been picking at kingfish in the 8 to 10 inch class along the Beach Haven and Ship Bottom fronts, best on the bottom two hours of the incoming when the surf is calm enough to hold bottom without a ton of lead. Nothing to write home about size-wise but it's steady action for anyone dragging kids to the beach with a rod.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August, which should sharpen current everywhere from the inlets to the bridge structure — that usually tightens up both the fluke bite in the rips and the after-dark bass bite around structure. If the bunker keep holding along the beachfront the way they have this week, I'd expect the blitz windows to keep firing through the weekend, especially with calm winds forecast. If I only had one trip, I'd fish Holgate or Beach Haven Inlet at first light for blues, then circle back after dark to the Route 72 bridge for bass on the outgoing. Watch the wind — anything out of the east chops up those beachfront blitzes fast.
